winner: Launch Window (to be renamed; working title "Doorhorn"), rebuilt as a full-day mission-control musical: the morning Launch, the daytime Request Line, and the nightly Re-entry with sung End Credits.
runner_ups: Dreadlines (renamed) — the avoidance-only list with aging monsters and the song-as-contract; the showrunner's #1 and the recommended second app, with its hero mechanic grafted into the winner as 'Hold items'

Split Level (renamed) — the nightly 90-second household sitcom with End Credits sung from the real task log and the lit dollhouse card; its credits and nightly artifact are grafted into the winner's Re-entry
elevator_pitch: The song is the schedule. A deadpan mission-control comedy lives in your phone and runs one launch a day: yours. At T-minus twelve a flight director calls it, a piece of music carries the whole house through wake, dress, and manifest, the janitor sings what you need to bring ("library book, the good water bottle, keys last seen kitchen counter"), and when the horns come in, shoes go on. Nobody looks at a screen and nobody has to say it twice. Through the day the same station plays songs exactly as long as the boring waits (two minutes of teeth with the cues sung in, ninety seconds of microwave). At night Re-entry dims the house to bed and rolls sung End Credits from what actually happened, top billing to whoever carried the day. Bad mornings get Scrub, a toddler-sized abort robot who declares "weather" and files no penalty. One phone, one speaker, no accounts, no subscription, one purchase.
why_it_wins: It is the only concept in the dossier that removes a chore instead of adding a ritual: the organized adult stops being the human clock, and the app is used twice a day, every day, structurally, without anyone remembering to open it, which is the strongest retention shape a paid app can have. It attaches to two events that already exist (leaving the house, going to bed) and, with the Request Line graft, to a dozen more (teeth, kettle, microwave, shower) that require zero new time. Three of four judges ranked it first and the everyday panel called it the clear winner ("I am the human clock"). Willingness to pay is already proven by the market: parents pay $36-50 a year for routine apps they resent and $189-369 for hardware that plays a song when a routine ends, while Lickety Split has fourteen years of reviews begging for exactly the chained multi-phase version. The mechanic (an authored section map that makes a piece of music the timer, the cue, and the role call) is unclaimed on iOS; every adjacent feature exists somewhere but nobody combines them and nobody works listen-only from one phone on a kitchen speaker. It is the most buildable concept for a solo local-first developer (one phone, no sync, no server, no runtime AI) and the one where music is literally the product rather than the mood, which is the most honest answer to the Suno mandate. Its two documented weaknesses, family-shelf confinement and modest vibrancy, are exactly what the grafts below fix: the Request Line makes it daily for anyone who brushes their teeth, and the Split Level End Credits give it the nightly shareable artifact and the 9/10 visual identity it lacked.
problems_solved: One adult runs the household as the human clock, repeating instructions and absorbing the resentment; no product moves the nagging off the person and onto something the room can hear.

Transitions (stop screens, get dressed, shoes, car; then tidy, teeth, book, lights) are the hardest minutes for kids and for many adults, and silent timers and checklists do not carry a room through them.
The manifest (lunch, permission slip, gym bag, keys) lives in one person's head; nothing reads it aloud at the exact moment it matters or remembers where the keys were last seen.
Routine apps are per-person checklists on subscription that must be looked at, tapped, and policed, so they become one more thing the organized person manages, and they hand a child a screen.

The one-to-five-minute dead zones of the day (two minutes of teeth, the microwave, the kettle, the shower) default to doomscrolling because nothing is composed to exactly that length with the cues built in.
Bedtime has the morning's problem in reverse and no shared wind-down cue that is not a lecture; the day ends without a boundary or a record.
Invisible labor (who remembered the photo money, who packed the bag) gets no credit and every attempt to count it turns into a scoreboard.
Bad mornings are logged as failure by streak apps; nobody gives a household an official, blameless reason ('weather') and a shorter plan for tomorrow.

grafted_ideas.idea: Re-entry ends with sung End Credits assembled from the day's real manifest and scrub log, billing order computed from carried load with the guest star always getting the best line; the lit launch tower on indigo is the nightly shareable card. No numbers, no percentages, only billing order and one written joke.

The Request Line: a library of exact-length songs for the day's boring waits (2:00 teeth with 'top left, top right, switch' sung into the lyrics, 1:30 microwave, 3:00 kettle, 5:00 shower with a rinse bridge at 4:30), so the app is daily for a solo commuter with zero new time, and the ON AIR bulb plus a shrinking vinyl in the Dynamic Island replaces any countdown.

The product rule and App Store subtitle: 'No clock. The job ends when the song ends.' No countdown digits anywhere except the parent's Live Activity, plus bar-aligned stems assembled on-device so an 8-minute and a 15-minute launch are one asset set and arrangements never repeat exactly.

The Stem Roll Call, run in-house with no network: each crew role (Pilot, Navigator, Cargo, Ground Crew) owns one stem of the launch track; tapping your patch or the one phone's roll-call buttons punches your stem in, and T-0 is the first time all stems play together. Silence is audible; showing up completes the song.

'The tap is the downbeat': every phase change, roll-call confirm and Scrub tap is quantized to the next bar boundary so signature moments never glitch, and the mission log records launches in bars, not minutes.

Hold items: the manifest can carry exactly one avoided task that ages visibly and affectionately ('dentist call, day 23, still on the manifest'), read in-song by the janitor with total neutrality; clearing it earns a victory sting and an amnesty verb lets you declare it dead of natural causes. Growth caps at day 30.

Walk-up cues as identity: each household member picks a five-second personal cue (mariachi, surf, marching band) that fires in the manifest bridge, so the reluctant partner's on-ramp is 'I want the mariachi one' rather than an onboarding flow.

Bail shrinks the job: a scrubbed launch automatically offers the next-shorter track tomorrow, the streak is untouched because there is no streak, and Scrub's 'weather' report is the crew regrouping, never a failure.

The hard ending with a receipt: Re-entry's final bar is a real buzzer-and-lights-off sting, and the day comes out as a folded card on a clothesline widget so the week is visible without opening the app.

iOS 26 scheduled Live Activities with an AlertConfiguration start tomorrow's launch with zero server, and Re-entry uses the tempo-ramp idea in reverse: BPM descends over twenty minutes toward resting pulse.

Ratings, not streaks: the mission log is a rolling 'on time 42 of 50 launches' that dips but never resets, yesterday is always correctable, and the overnight StandBy mode is a color-bars-style Hangar screen that looks like nothing else on the store.

Season Two candidate, not v1: a thirty-second 'Fuel' segment at 5 p.m. where the crew settles dinner from the house menu with one veto, feeding the manifest and the End Credits. Held back to protect the v1 scope.

core_loop: 6:58 a.m. The launch was scheduled last night (AlarmKit alarm plus a scheduled Live Activity), so the phone on the counter or the HomePod simply starts: a 30-second station ID, then Flight Director Augustine Pell: 'T-minus twelve. Launch window open.' The launch track is the plan. Verse one is wake and wash (the Request Line's two-minute teeth song is nested here with quadrant cues sung in), the first key change is get dressed, the bridge is the manifest, where Gus the janitor sings today's list from the household's own edits ('lunchbox, library book, the good water bottle, keys last seen kitchen counter, and the dentist call, day 23, still on the manifest'), and the final chorus with the horns means shoes and door. During the bridge the Stem Roll Call runs: each crew member taps their patch on the one phone (or their own phone if the household shares) and their stem punches in on the next bar; at T-0 every stem plays together and the liftoff fanfare logs a clean launch. If it goes badly, anyone presses Scrub, the abort robot declares 'weather', the day is logged without penalty, and tomorrow's launch offers the next-shorter track. The parent's Lock Screen and StandBy show a huge cutout countdown and the phase name; nobody else looks at a screen. Through the day the Request Line takes taps or a Shortcut/NFC tag: 'Microwave 1:30', 'Kettle', 'Shower', and the station serves a song exactly that long while the crew does a bit (Dr. Farrago forecasting catastrophe for a kitchen). 8:15 p.m. Re-entry: Bunny Kowalczyk's late-night voice runs the same phase structure in reverse over a twenty-minute track whose tempo descends (tidy, teeth, book, lights), and the final bar is a buzzer and the house going dark. Then the End Credits roll: a sixty-second sung credits sequence over the lit launch tower, billing order computed from the manifest and who carried it, guest star gets the best line, and the card hangs on the clothesline widget. Sunday runs a two-minute Flight Review with the week's launches, scrubs, and the crew's notes, and a no-launch lounge track for mornings with nowhere to be.
first_60_seconds: No account, no household setup. Screen one is the annotated score itself: a colored waveform with phase bands (WAKE, DRESS, MANIFEST, DOOR) and a horn marker labeled 'shoes and door', so the reviewer and the parent see in five seconds that this is a score, not a timer. One question: 'When do you need to be out the door?' Pick 7:40. Then a button: 'Test fire (60 seconds).' It runs a miniature launch on the spot: Augustine calls T-minus one, Gus sings a three-item demo manifest that ends with 'and your keys, wherever they are', the horns come in, and the fanfare fires when you tap the door. That is the moment the person laughs and understands the product. The app then asks two optional things: 'Who's launching?' (add names to crew patches, or skip; a solo user is automatically Pilot, Ground Crew and audience) and 'Play tomorrow on a speaker?' (AirPlay picker). It closes with 'Tomorrow at 7:28, Augustine will call it. You don't need to open the app.' The free tier's three Request Line songs (teeth, microwave, kettle) are shown as tiles so the value continues before the first morning.
daily_return_hooks: The morning launch starts itself at the scheduled time (AlarmKit + scheduled Live Activity), so the return is structural rather than remembered; the household hears it whether or not anyone opens the app.
Re-entry at bedtime is the second structural anchor, with the same phase grammar in reverse and a hard buzzer ending the day.
The Request Line rides on waits that already happen: teeth twice a day, the microwave, the kettle, the shower, each with a song exactly that long and cues sung in.
The manifest has memory ('keys last seen kitchen counter', 'library book due Thursday'), so editing tonight's manifest is a nightly thirty-second habit with a payoff at 7 a.m.
The End Credits card is a once-a-day artifact people screenshot and send ('top billing: whoever remembered the photo money'), hung on a clothesline widget that shows the week.
The Hold item ages one day at a time and the janitor reads it every morning without judgment, which is a gentle daily reason to clear it.
Ratings, not streaks: the mission log shows 'on time 42 of 50 launches' and lets you fix yesterday, so a bad week never breaks the habit.
Sunday Flight Review: a two-minute recap with the crew's notes and the week's launches in color, scrubs in greyscale.
Seasonal and holiday flavors (marching band in September, a snow-day lounge in December) and Dr. Farrago's forecast being wrong in a new way every day.
feature_pillars: Song-as-schedule launches: an authored section map per track (phase timestamps, role-cue markers, the horn entry that means door), five durations and multiple flavors assembled on-device from bar-aligned stems, driving the Live Activity, StandBy countdown, and AirPlay/HomePod playback from one phone.

The Manifest with memory and one Hold item: household-edited, read in-song by the janitor mid-track, with 'last seen' memory and a single avoided task that ages affectionately and can be cleared or amnestied.

Stem Roll Call and crew patches: each member owns a role, a color, a five-second walk-up cue, and a stem of the launch track; T-0 is the first time all stems play together. Works pass-the-phone with no sync; optional CloudKit household share later.

Re-entry and End Credits: a descending-tempo bedtime track with the phase grammar reversed, a buzzer that ends the day, and sung credits assembled from the real manifest with billing order computed from carried load, delivered as a joke, never a number.

The Request Line: exact-length songs with cues sung into the lyrics for the day's micro-waits, launchable from a widget, Shortcut, Action Button or NFC tag, no Apple Music subscription required, fully offline.

Scrub and the Mission Log: a blameless abort with 'weather' as the official reason, automatic shorter track tomorrow, a rolling on-time rating that never resets, editable yesterday, and a Sunday Flight Review.
original_world_and_cast_sketch: Cul-de-Sac Mission Control is a decommissioned county launch authority that lost its rockets in a budget cut and now runs exactly one launch a day: yours. The bunker sits, in flat saturated color, under a launch tower that rises from an ordinary kitchen counter; the sky behind it shifts from deep indigo at T-12 to gold at the manifest bridge to hot orange in the final chorus and a clean white flash at liftoff, and inverts to dusk purple and lamp-glow amber for Re-entry. Everyone in the building is incompetent except the janitor. The cast: Augustine Pell, Flight Director, who has never raised her voice, speaks only in checklists, and believes any morning is survivable with a procedure. Gus Marchetti, Janitor and de facto Payload Specialist, the only person who knows where anything is, who sings the manifest with the calm of a man who has seen every lunchbox; he is the emotional center and the one the household comes to trust. Dr. Ines Farrago, Meteorologist, who forecasts catastrophe every morning, has been wrong every day since 1998, and regards this as a streak worth protecting. Bunny Kowalczyk, Countdown Announcer, a late-night jazz voice who runs Re-entry and insists on calling bedtime 'splashdown'. Lionel Abara, CAPCOM, whose entire job is to say 'copy' and who has started saying it at home. And Scrub, a toddler-sized abort robot with one big button, who declares 'weather' as the official reason for every scrubbed launch and is the character kids will draw. The recurring antagonist is an invented bureaucracy, the Department of Five More Minutes, which issues delay permits nobody applied for, with its Board of Snooze Appeals. Satire targets countdown melodrama and bureaucracy, never real agencies, brands or people: no NASA insignia, no Apollo-era likenesses, no real call signs. The register is Bob's-Burgers warmth at a 4+/9+ rating, not South Park edge; the crew never blames the household, and the comedy lives in lyrics and short cues because at 6:58 a.m. nobody is looking at a screen. Characters are hard-shaped flat cutouts with one strong silhouette and one signature color each, no paper grain, no cutout jitter, no mitten hands, designed to survive tinted and clear icon modes; crew patches are bold circular badges in each member's color. Names must be grepped against real public figures before shipping.
music_system: Music is the product, not the mood, and the system is built to survive Suno's September 2026 terms. (1) Section maps are data: every track ships with a developer-authored JSON map (phase timestamps, cue bars, role-cue markers, the horn entry) stored as versioned data, which is copyrightable, so the map and lyrics carry the protectable value while the audio is treated as a replaceable layer. (2) Launch tracks are one original melody, developer-written lyrics, rendered through Suno v6 Covers into six flavors at v1 (marching band, surf, disco, big band, bluegrass, lullaby for Re-entry), each generated at a locked BPM and split with Advanced Split into calm/medium/intense layers plus four role stems (drums, bass, brass, choir) for the Stem Roll Call. Stems ship as bar-trimmed CAF and are assembled on-device with AVAudioEngine so the five durations (8, 10, 12, 15, 20 minutes) are arrangements of one asset set, never separate downloads, and arrangements vary daily so the 300th morning is not the first. (3) The Request Line is a library of exact-length songs with the cues sung in: 2:00 teeth (quadrant switches at :30), 1:00, 1:30, 3:00, 5:00 shower with a rinse bridge at 4:30, 10:00, each in two or three flavors, rotated so nothing repeats within a week. (4) Re-entry tracks descend roughly 20 BPM over twenty minutes and end on a buzzer; the End Credits are one template song with modular sung lines per manifest item and role, pre-generated per line in the same voice lane, assembled at runtime. (5) Each character has a musical genre lane rather than a voice lock (Augustine: brass and snare; Gus: warm baritone folk; Farrago: theremin-flecked lounge; Bunny: late-night jazz; Scrub: kazoo and toy piano), because Suno Voices preserve an essence, not a lock, and lanes make drift invisible. (6) Sounds-mode stings: liftoff fanfare, Scrub klaxon, victory sting for a cleared Hold item, a dozen micro tap sounds. Budget: about 45 paid downloads for a working beta and about 110 by launch, two Premier months plus Studio for stems and uncapped exports; every track generated only on the licensed v6 line while subscribed, with dated receipts, prompts and download logs archived off-platform; no artist names or 'in the style of' prompts, no Remix, no watermark stripping (keep unmodified originals alongside the CAF derivatives). Every lyric and script is written by the developer and registered with the Copyright Office as a literary collection; within the first year the station ID, liftoff fanfare and the launch melody are re-recorded with a human musician so the brand owns at least one defensible audio asset. Disclose plainly in About: 'Every line written by a person. Songs produced with Suno from those lyrics.' Envato Elements supplies layout references, UI scaffolding, halftone and poster templates, and font shortlists only; no Envato font is embedded unless its item license permits app embedding (default to OFL faces), and no character, patch or icon is built from stock art.
what_you_pay_for: Free, complete in itself and enough to prove it on the first morning: one launch flavor at 10 and 12 minutes, one Re-entry track, the manifest with memory and one Hold item, Scrub and the mission log, the Test Fire, and three Request Line songs (teeth 2:00, microwave 1:30, kettle 3:00). One-time $9.99 unlock under the Small Business Program: every flavor and duration, crew roles with walk-up cues and the Stem Roll Call, the full Request Line library, End Credits with the shareable card and clothesline widget, ninety-day mission log history and Sunday Flight Review, the weekend lounge and Hangar StandBy mode, and household sharing via iCloud when it ships. Seasonal flavor drops are free updates, never a subscription; no ads, no accounts, no lost streaks because there are no streaks. The paywall says exactly that. Positioned against Routinery ($36/yr), Brili ($49.99/yr) and $189-369 routine hardware, and marketed to roommates, couples and solo commuters as well as families so it is never shelved as a kids' timer.
name_candidates: Cul-de-Sac Mission Control (long form; 'CMC' or 'Mission Cul-de-Sac' as the store name)

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Name: 'Launch Window' is a 2026 Steam game, an LLC, and a generic aerospace term that App Store search maps to rocket trackers; every candidate above is unverified because USPTO lookups were blocked in the hunt.
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: Coin the name before any asset is drawn; run Trademark Center knock-outs in Classes 9, 41 and 42, App Store Connect availability in every storefront, and domain checks; file intent-to-use on the winner. Keep 'assemble', 'endgame', 'infinity' and any show name out of the name, subtitle, keywords and IAP names.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Apple's June 2026 4.3(b) rewrite names 'simple timers' as a saturated category subject to rejection and removal; a reviewer will compare the app to Routinery, Brili, ReadySet and Prep Pal.
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: The annotated score (phase bands, role-cue markers, the horn labeled 'shoes and door') is screen one and screenshot one; metadata leads with original music, the manifest, the crew and household mode and never says 'timer' or 'alarm'; Notes for Review name the section map, Stem Roll Call, in-song manifest and End Credits as the meaningful difference; list under Lifestyle or Productivity with Entertainment secondary.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Family-shelf confinement: three judges scored broad appeal 6; the retiree did not need it and the app could be filed with kids' timers.
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: The Request Line (teeth, microwave, kettle, shower) makes it daily for solo people with zero new time; a solo user is automatically Pilot, Ground Crew and audience; marketing leads with roommates, couples, shift workers and solo commuters alongside families; never opt into the Kids Category; the parent's phone is the primary device.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Music fatigue: the same launch at 7 a.m. 300 times a year, and Chompers and Mimizaur both died on content exhaustion.
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: On-device arrangement from stems so no two mornings are identical, six flavors at v1 with seasonal drops, a rotation rule that never repeats a Request Line song within a week, a quiet mode (spoken cues and stings only, still real audio, never a silent session), and the crew's daily lines living in short cues that are cheap to expand.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Suno legal exposure: purely AI-generated audio is uncopyrightable, Suno disclaims copyright and indemnity, commercial rights attach only to paid-tier downloads capped at 60 a month on Premier, UMG/Sony filed a second suit on 18 September 2026 and GEMA won in Munich in July; a model withdrawal could make outputs unshippable.
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: Treat audio as a replaceable layer beneath copyrightable lyrics, scripts, section maps, characters and code; write and register every lyric; generate only on the licensed v6 line while subscribed, never with artist names, with dated receipts and logs archived off-platform; keep unmodified originals; re-record the station ID, fanfare and launch melody with a human musician in year one; keep a regeneration plan on another licensed provider; disclose in-app.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: AlarmKit and Live Activity constraints: custom alarm sounds are capped at about 30 seconds, the system always shows a Stop button, scheduled Live Activities need iOS 26, HomePod/AirPlay latency skews timing, and Live Activities may not carry promotion.
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: iOS 26 floor; the alarm is a 30-second station ID with a secondary 'Open the launch' App Intent and the full track plays in-app on AirPlay; derive Live Activity timing from playback position, not the wall clock; the Live Activity shows only countdown, phase and role; background audio only while a track actually plays.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Scope creep: the grafts (Request Line, End Credits, Stem Roll Call, Hold items) could push a five-out-of-five buildability project past a year for one person.
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: Phase the build: v1 is launches, Re-entry, manifest, Scrub, mission log and three Request Line songs on one phone (about four months); v1.1 adds the full Request Line and End Credits card; v1.2 adds crew stems and walk-up cues; CloudKit household share and the 5 p.m. Fuel segment are Season Two. Ship when the first morning proves the feel, not when the world is complete.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Tone drift: mission-control comedy sliding into South Park edge, a weather character reading as a famous bumbling weatherman, or the End Credits reading as passive-aggressive scorekeeping.
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: Write to a 4+/9+ rating with satire aimed only at invented institutions; make Dr. Farrago specific (a streak-keeper who is proud of being wrong, not a dim sidekick) and check silhouettes against known characters; the credits show billing order and one joke, never a number, and the guest star always gets the best line; playtest with the reluctant partner in the room.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Age rating and child devices: iOS 27 Child Accounts put downloads behind Ask to Buy and any crude humor jumps the rating to 13+, hiding it from family devices.
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: Honest 4+/9+ questionnaire answers, no profanity or alcohol in the default script, parent-owned Productivity/Lifestyle listing, no data collection from anyone, 'Data Not Collected' privacy label.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: The everyday panel's quiet worry: music at 6:58 a.m. is divisive, and the crew's comedy is invisible when nobody looks at a screen.
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: Jokes live in lyrics and five-second cues; volume ramps in over the first eight bars; per-household 'first sound' choice (station ID, soft brass, spoken checklist); the Hangar mode and the End Credits card give the world a visual life at night when people are looking.

judge_dissent: The raw sum put Launch Window first by four points (221 to Dreadlines' 217, Split Level 213), but the judges did not agree on the order. The comedy showrunner ranked Dreadlines first (59) and Launch Window third (57), on the grounds that Dreadlines' monsters generate cast from the user's own life without a writer typing a line, that its 'my dentist monster is 41 days old' share line is the best sentence in the dossier, and that it should absorb Pull It Off's bar-quantized score and Caper's script library as the single avoidance greenlight. The indie publisher tied the two at 53, favoring Launch Window only on tiebreak for buildability and proven willingness to pay. The everyday panel (57 vs 53) and the product strategist (54 vs 52) put Launch Window clearly first: it removes a chore rather than adding a ritual, runs twice daily without anyone opening the app, and is the one concept where music is the product. All four agreed Split Level had the best cast and the strongest visual identity but the heaviest authoring load and a homage-stacking problem. Two cross-cutting dissents were also raised: the panel and strategist flagged Launch Window's family skew and 4.3(b) timer exposure, and the showrunner flagged that its comedy runs at dawn when nobody looks at a screen. Resolution: Launch Window wins because the brief's hardest criteria are 'part of daily lives' and 'anyone can use it' at a price people will pay once, and it is the only concept that satisfies the first structurally (two unavoidable daily events, zero new time) and the second by removing the need for anyone else to install anything, while being the most buildable and the most honest use of Suno. The showrunner's case is honored by grafting Dreadlines' hero mechanic into the manifest as the aging Hold item, Pull It Off's bar-quantized taps into the engine, and by naming Dreadlines (renamed) the recommended second product in the same world's sound. The family-skew and dawn-comedy objections are answered by the Request Line graft (daily for solo people, jokes in exact-length daytime songs) and the Split Level End Credits graft (a nightly visual artifact when people are actually looking). The 4.3(b) exposure is answered by making the annotated score the first screen and first screenshot. Every judge required a rename; that is treated as the price of admission, not a tiebreaker.
